New York Jets Performance Lab 2026

This overview is a simple, up-to-date summary of how the Jets are performing this season. EPA per play estimates how each play changes a team’s scoring chances; success rate shows how often a play makes enough progress for its situation. They add context that points and yards alone can miss, accounting for factors such as down, distance and field position to show the value and consistency of the plays. The chart pop-ups explain each measure in more detail. Use this page for the season’s big picture, then explore the Offence, Defence, Opposition, Trends & Forecasts, Coverage & Schemes and other pages for a closer look at particular parts of the team.

Season snapshot

  • Offence: Across the season through Week 9, the offence averages +0.003 EPA per play (rank 15 of 32), close to league average. EPA per play estimates how each play shifts scoring chances. The last-three-game average is +0.062, but that hides a sharp latest-game dip: after Week 7 +0.272, Week 8 +0.250, offence fell to -0.302 in Week 9, with passing (-0.292) and rushing (-0.317) both below zero.
  • Defence: Defence remains the bigger season-long gap: opponents gain +0.039 EPA per play on average (rank 22 of 32). The last three weekly results were Week 7 +0.283, Week 8 +0.212, Week 9 +0.166; opponent EPA fell across the stretch, but opponents still gained scoring value on average in all three games. The last-three-game average is +0.220.
  • Passing defence: The clearest passing warning came in Week 7 against MIA: the Jets allowed +0.661 EPA per pass above that opponent’s average against other defences. This is a single-game comparison, not a full schedule-strength measure; play-by-play data does not show coverage calls or individual assignments.

Defensive Coverage Intelligence

Directly charted pass-dropback coverage labels are present for 2018–2025. Joined participation/PBP records exist for 2016, 2017, but those seasons contain no usable coverage labels and are excluded from coverage tables. The latest labelled season is 2025; 2026 play-level coverage calls are not released until after the postseason. 2018–2022 labelled data originate from NFL Next Gen Stats via nflverse; 2023 onward labelled data originate from FTN Data via nflverse. Treat the provider transition as a methodological break. Rates use labelled plays as denominators; EPA and pressure are descriptive, not causal. No coverage labels are inferred.

Advanced data availability and limitations

The following fields are not available in the current free 2026 play-by-play source. No proxy assignment or invented personnel label is used.

offense_personnelNot present in the current 2026 PBP file
defense_personnelNot present in the current 2026 PBP file
offense_player_participationNo complete on-field player list per play in the current PBP file
defense_player_participationNo complete on-field player list per play in the current PBP file
coverage_assignmentNo play-level defender-to-receiver responsibility field
coverage_shell_2026No play-level coverage label in the current free 2026 feed
  • Weather splits are game-level and descriptive, not causal
  • No player-combination impact is calculated without complete per-play participation
  • No personnel-package split is calculated without explicit package fields
  • No coverage responsibility is inferred from tackles, interceptions or proximity

Expanding-window historical backtest

Lower MAE and RMSE indicate better forecasts. Every prediction uses only games completed before its target week.

Validation: The backtest does not show a consistent advantage over the league-average baseline. Treat these forecasts as exploratory context, not a validated predictive model; the model should not drive decisions on its own.

Model: 60% play-weighted mean of latest three team games + 40% play-weighted season-to-date mean; shrink 20% toward play-weighted league mean.

  • Early-season sample sizes are small and forecasts are descriptive baselines, not calibrated probabilities
  • Backtest uses expanding time windows and excludes the target week from all inputs
  • EPA is volatile; the model should only be retained if it improves on the league-average baseline
  • Defensive EPA is opponent EPA allowed per play; lower is better

Interpretation limits

  • Pressure deployment splits are descriptive associations, not causal estimates
  • n_blitzers counts blitzers; n_pass_rushers counts all pass rushers. A five-rusher play commonly includes four defensive linemen plus one blitzer.
  • Small categories should not be interpreted without considering their play counts
  • Snap counts measure player deployment and are not per-play player attribution or coverage responsibility
  • A QB hit or sack event is not a complete pressure chart or pass-rush win measure

Opponent-adjusted game context

Opponent baseline is that opponent's passing EPA against every defence other than the Jets. Positive adjusted values mean the opponent performed better against the Jets than against its other opponents.

Coverage attribution and limits

  • Only 2026 FTN-charted passing plays matched to nflverse PBP are used for deployment splits.
  • Opponent adjustment is descriptive and does not control for quarterback, injuries, game state, protection or play-calling.
  • Pressure counts describe rush deployment, not time-to-pressure or individual pass-rush wins.
  • Explosive pass is defined as 20+ yards; YAC explosive proxy is 10+ yards after catch.
  • No reliable public 2026 play-level coverage-shell or defender-to-receiver assignment field was found in the available sources; coverage effectiveness cannot be attributed to individual defenders or shells.
  • Small deployment and situational groups should be interpreted cautiously.

Interpretation limits

  • PFR snap counts show player exposure by game, not the exact 11 defenders on each charted passing play.
  • Weekly position-group snap shares are aggregate exposure and cannot establish which personnel were on the field for a given play.
  • Injury report statuses are not treated as proof of game absence; actual snap counts are the better participation measure.
  • Week-level relationships are descriptive and are not causal player-impact estimates.
  • Injury-to-snap reconciliation uses normalized names; unmatched injury entries are retained.
  • Zero recorded defensive snaps does not prove a player was inactive; the snap feed cannot distinguish inactivity from non-use.
  • The current public FTN 2026 feed has no reliable play-level defender participation or coverage responsibility assignments.

Defensive player production relative to workload

Production rates use only defensive snaps from weeks with a corresponding weekly player-stat row. Total snaps include all recorded snap-count weeks; stat-record snaps and coverage percentage show how much workload is represented. Missing weekly stat rows remain blank, not zero. Rates are descriptive, not player grades, and should be compared within similar roles.

Data coverage and limitations

Identity-resolved snap player-weeks: 159 of 159 (100.0%). Weekly box-score rows present: 140; no weekly stat row: 19. Total snap exposure: 6567; stat-record snap exposure: 6296 (95.9%). Missing stat rows are not zero production.

  • Weekly defensive statistics are official box-score production, not charted player-level pressure or coverage impact.
  • QB hits and sacks are recorded outcomes; they do not capture every pressure or pass-rush win.
  • Rates per 100 defensive snaps are descriptive workload normalizations, not causal or position-adjusted player grades.
  • Tackles and passes defended depend on role, opponent play volume and opportunity; comparisons across positions are not direct quality rankings.
  • Weekly GSIS player IDs are used for the primary snap-to-stat join; unique exact player-name matches are used only where a snap ID is missing.
  • A resolved snap record can have no weekly box-score row; this is distinguished from an unresolved identity and does not imply inactivity.
  • Weekly production fields remain missing when no weekly player-stat row exists; they are not converted to zero.
  • Season per-snap production rates use only snaps from weeks with a corresponding player-stat row; total snaps and stat-record snap coverage are shown separately.

Offensive personnel availability and deployment

Weekly offensive snap exposure describes who was used and how workloads changed; it does not identify the exact formation or personnel grouping on each play.

Interpretation limits

  • PFR snap counts measure player exposure by game, not exact personnel group or formation on each play.
  • Position-group shares are sums of player snaps; because multiple players share a play, interpret as workload composition rather than mutually exclusive shares of 11 players.
  • Injury statuses are not proof of game absence; snap counts are used as observed participation.
  • Zero recorded offensive snaps does not prove a player was inactive.
  • Injury-to-snap reconciliation uses normalized player names; unmatched entries are retained.
  • Offensive line player IDs may be missing in the PFR-to-GSIS crosswalk; unmatched production is reported separately.

Offensive player production relative to workload

Production rates use only offensive snaps from weeks with a corresponding weekly player-stat row. Total snaps include all recorded snap-count weeks; stat-record snaps and coverage percentage show how much workload is represented. Missing weekly stat rows remain blank, not zero. Quarterback efficiency is separated from skill-player workload rates; comparisons should be made within role.

Data coverage and limitations

Identity-resolved snap player-weeks: 155 of 155 (100.0%). Weekly box-score rows present: 104; no weekly stat row: 51. Total snap exposure: 6127; stat-record snap exposure: 3936 (64.2%). Missing stat rows are not zero production.

  • Official weekly box-score and EPA fields are combined with PFR offensive snap exposure.
  • Snap-normalized rates describe output per workload; they are not player grades or causal estimates.
  • Quarterback passing EPA per attempt is a separate efficiency measure; yards per snap is not a quarterback efficiency metric.
  • Receiving yards per target and rushing/receiving production depend on role, play design and opportunity.
  • Offensive line output is assessed through snap exposure and team-level results; individual blocking grades are not available in the free sources.
  • Stable GSIS IDs are used where available; unique normalized player names from the weekly roster and player-stat feeds fill missing crosswalks. Ambiguous names remain unresolved.
  • A resolved snap record can have no weekly box-score row, particularly an offensive lineman with no recorded box-score event; this is distinguished from an unresolved player identity.
  • Weekly production fields remain missing when no weekly player-stat row exists; they are not converted to zero.
  • Season per-snap production rates use only snaps from weeks with a corresponding player-stat row; total snaps and stat-record snap coverage are shown separately.

Analysis controls

Filters apply to visible dashboard tables where matching columns exist.

Player evaluation — role-adjusted measures

Offence: compare QB passing EPA/attempt; RB yards and touches per 100 snaps; WR/TE receiving yards per target and targets per 100 snaps. Defence: compare DL disruption events and QB hits per 100 snaps; LB/DB tackles, passes defended and interceptions alongside snap share. Do not rank OL on box-score rates: individual blocking grades are unavailable.

Rates are workload normalisations, not grades or causal estimates. Consider games played, role, opportunity and matched-week coverage.

Opponent rushing by direction

Run direction is recorded from the ball-carrier’s offensive perspective, so “right” means the opposing offence ran toward its right. EPA allowed per run above the NFL average indicates more scoring value gained by opponents. Each split shows its play count; outcomes do not identify an individual defender’s assignment.

Metric guide

These are play-level measures, so they describe team performance by situation. They complement familiar totals like points and yards, which do not show how valuable or repeatable each play was. Use the chart pop-ups for the specific chart definitions and the notes below for how to read the measures together.

MeasureWhat it meansWhat it adds
EPA per playThe estimated change in scoring value created by an average play. A positive offensive value adds expected points; a negative value reduces them.It accounts for the down, distance and field position around a play, so it distinguishes efficient plays from yards gained when little is at stake.
Defensive EPA allowedThe EPA value opponents gain against the defence. Lower or negative values mean the defence is reducing opponents’ expected scoring.It puts plays in context instead of treating every yard or first down as equally valuable.
Success rateThe share of plays that meet a down-specific progress benchmark: roughly 40% of yards needed on first down, 60% on second, and all remaining yards on third or fourth.It shows how often the team stays on schedule. EPA shows the size of each play’s impact; success rate shows how consistently plays make useful progress.
EPA by pass or runEPA per play split by whether the play was a pass or a run.This helps show which part of the offence or defence is driving the overall result.
Opponent-adjusted EPAA game result compared with that opponent’s average performance in its other games.It adds a schedule context check; one game is not a complete schedule-strength rating.

EPA is a model-based estimate, not points actually scored. Small samples, penalties, turnovers and game context can affect the result. Player tables also depend on each source’s coverage.

ESPN Total QBR — Jets quarterbacks

ESPN Total QBR is a separate, context-adjusted quarterback metric. It is not the traditional passer rating and should be read alongside EPA/play, completion efficiency, pressure and the team’s overall offensive output. Missing ESPN QBR rows for Jets game weeks: 4. Missing values are not imputed.
